newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan boosts guard after U.S. mission stoned.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan boosts guard after U.S. mission stoned.

text.p: Pakistani authorities tightened security around diplomatic missions on Thursday after demonstrators attacked the U.S. consulate in Lahore overnight in protest at American missile strikes on Iraq, police said.

The National Assembly (lower house of parliament) also passed a resolution on Thursday expressing its shock at the U.S. strikes, which some opposition deputies called aggression against a fellow Islamic state.

"We have tightened security, increased mobile patrols and checkpoints in Islamabad after this crisis," Police Superintendent Raja Nawaz told Reuters. "Security has been beefed up at all installations, including embassies."

About 100 members of the student wing of the religious Jamaat-i-Islami party threw stones at the U.S. consulate in Lahore on Wednesday night. Guards fired in the air to disperse them. There were no casualties and little damage.
Witnesses said extra police were guarding the U.S. consulate, American Centre and British Council office in Lahore on Thursday, but there were no reports of fresh violence.

The U.S. embassy issued a security notice on Wednesday, advising Americans to observe personal security precautions after the missile strike on Iraq, which it said could lead to attacks on U.S. citizens or interests in Pakistan.
The Assembly resolution read: "This house expresses its deep concern and shock at the United States missile strikes against selected defence targets in Iraq"

"We must stand up against this aggression otherwise we will also become a target of American hegemony," opposition deputy Mehmud Khan Achakzai said. "This is a war between Islam and Kufr (infidelity)," said another, Qazi Fazlullah.
Pakistan, which projects itself as a moderate Islamic country, has twice voiced concern at the U.S. action, urging all parties to exercise restraint and avoid the use of force.
Islamabad sent troops to help defend Saudi Arabia during the 1990-91 Gulf crisis, although popular opinion at home at the time strongly favoured Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
Newspapers on Thursday condemned the latest American action against Iraq as a cynical election ploy by U.S. President Bill Clinton likely to lead to greater regional instability.
"The missile attack...was basically aimed at improving President Clinton's chances for re-election, rather than doing a noble deed," the English-language daily The News said.
The Frontier Post said the attacks were "excessive" and said they appeared to be linked to the U.S. presidential election.

The Karachi-based daily Dawn said the U.S.-Iraqi showdown was "popular theatre" in the United States at election time, but had blurred the distinction between a country's internal affairs and its offences against the world community.
